title: Rapture and return
hook: some Protestants expect believers to be caught up before tribulation; other Christians read 1 Thessalonians 4 differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bible's near-last words, and an old Aramaic one: maranatha. Your line was come, lord jesus. Where did the word come find you at the table? Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

A bumper sticker warns that the car may suddenly be driverless. A shelf of novels and films shows people vanishing mid-sentence, clothes left in a heap on the seat. Some Christians call that coming moment the rapture. Other Christians grew up in churches where it was never taught at all. Both are reading the same short passage, a few lines near the end of Paul's first letter to the church in Thessalonica. Today we read those lines slowly, and look at how differently they're read.

First, why Paul wrote it. Not to give a timetable. Some in the young church had died, and the living were grieving and afraid. Paul says: "I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." It begins as a letter to people at a graveside. Second, the picture: "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air." The word rapture isn't in the King James text. It says caught up. Third, the readings. Some Protestants, many of them dispensationalists, read this as a gathering of believers before a time of great tribulation, with Christ's visible return coming later. Other Christians, among them the Catholic and Orthodox churches and other Protestants, read it as part of Christ's one return at the end: the dead raised, the living gathered up to meet him. Some readers hear in that word meet a town going out to greet an arriving guest and walk him back in. On that reading, the meeting in the air is a welcome party. Fourth, the lines Paul ends on: "and so shall we ever be with the Lord. Wherefore comfort one another with these words." Whatever the timetable, Paul ends with together, and with comfort.

Here's the practice: read 1 Thessalonians chapter four, verses thirteen to eighteen. It's six verses. Read them before the bell, slowly, out loud if you can. Then settle, and breathe. Let one phrase stay with you: "comfort one another with these words." Bring to mind someone who is grieving, or someone you've lost. You don't need to settle any question about the end. Just sit with the people the letter was written for. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Rapture. A name, not in the King James text, for being caught up to meet the Lord in the air. Christians read the passage in more than one way.

Your line: ever with the lord. This week ran from all things new, through open gates, healing leaves and come, Lord Jesus, to this. Today, send one word of comfort to someone who's grieving. Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Some Protestant churches teach a rapture of believers before a time of tribulation; the Catholic and Orthodox churches and other Protestants read 1 Thessalonians 4 as part of Christ's one return, and some churches read the passage at funerals.

original.note: Greek: we shall be caught up, snatched away. 1 Thessalonians 4:17.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rapture means people vanishing and cars left driverless.
what it means: Paul tells grieving friends that the dead and the living will be caught up together to meet the Lord, and so be ever with him.
what a scholar hears: harpagesometha, we shall be snatched up; and a word for meet that some readers hear as a town going out to welcome a guest.
